title: You're Doing Lateral Raises Wrong! That's Why Your Shoulders Aren't Growing
channelDescription: Gym or calisthenics. Watch the videos.

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: Gym or calisthenics. Watch the videos.

text:
Track your reps on Symmetry, for free 👉🏼 https://symmetry.club/go/bluegains17

You do lateral raises every week, and your shoulders still look exactly the same. Your deltoid is the biggest muscle in your entire arm (bigger than your triceps and more than double your biceps), and the side of it is what makes you look wide. But the way most people raise, other muscles end up doing the job.

These are the 5 mistakes that keep your side delts small, what the science actually says about each one, and the whole fix in one rep. The last one is something most coaches get completely backwards.

Sources & Studies: https://rentry.co/7kmr778b

The 5 mistakes:

• Mistake 1, swinging: when you bounce from the knees and jerk with your lower back, your legs and back lift the weight, not your delts. A small push at the start is fine, a big swing isn't. Drop the weight and control the way down
• Mistake 2, going too high: the dumbbell is heaviest for your delts when your arm is parallel to the floor. Higher, and more of the job goes to your traps. Stop when your elbows reach shoulder height
• Mistake 3, the same weight and the same 10 reps for months: pick a weight you can lift 12-20 times with clean form and stop 1-2 reps short of failure. In a 2025 study, 10 hard sets a week grew the side delts about 4% in 8 weeks
• Mistake 4, shrugging: feeling your traps is normal (your shoulder blade rotates up about 50 degrees when you lift your arm). Creeping your shoulder up to your ear isn't. Push the dumbbells out, not up
• Mistake 5, pouring the can: tested on bodybuilders, pinky up didn't take work away from the side delts (thumbs up is the one that shifts it to the front delts), but a hard twist squeezes the tendon on top of your shoulder. Default: palms down, thumbs forward

The whole fix in one rep: slight bend in the elbows, palms down, thumbs forward, push out to the sides until your arms are parallel to the floor, shoulders away from your ears, no swing, control the way down. 12-20 reps close to failure, about 10 hard sets a week. Cables or dumbbells? In a 2025 study both grew the side delts about the same, so pick the one you'll actually do.

You're tired all day, your belly is growing, and your drive in the gym is gone. Your testosterone might be lower than it should be, and no, you don't need a booster: most of them do nothing. Five free habits bring it back to your normal, and one of them, if you get it wrong, costs you as much testosterone in one week as years of aging.

Across 24 studies, the more weight men lost, the more their testosterone went up. Men on low-fat diets had lower testosterone than men who ate more fat. Three beers a night for just three weeks dropped testosterone about 7%. Men in their 60s who had never trained raised theirs 17% in 12 weeks of lifting. And young men who slept 5 hours a night for one week lost 10-15% of their testosterone, with the biggest drop in the afternoon and evening, right when most people train.

Sources & Studies: https://rentry.co/g9uzqtzx

The 5 habits:

• Lose the extra fat: eat about 300-500 calories below maintenance, keep protein high and aim for about half a kilo a week. Keep lifting so you lose fat, not muscle. Watch the weekly average on the scale, not one day. Don't crash diet: getting extremely lean can drop it too
• Don't cut out fat: keep eggs, olive oil, nuts, meat and fish on your plate. About a quarter to a third of your calories from fat. Zinc or vitamin D only help if a blood test shows you're low
• Cut the heavy drinking: swap to alcohol-free beer and keep the real thing occasional
• Lift heavy and walk: squats, push-ups, rows and presses. 3-4 sets of 5-10 reps, 2-4 days a week, stop 1-2 reps before failure and add a little weight or one rep every week. On rest days, walk (8,000-10,000 steps)
• Sleep: 7-9 hours, wake up at the same time every day (even on weekends), a dark, cool room and no caffeine about 8 hours before bed

Give it 12 weeks. You don't need a booster, you need a bedtime.

This video is educational, not medical advice. If you think your testosterone is low, ask your doctor for a blood test.

Find a bar, grab it, lift your feet. No reps, no weight, nothing moves. It's the most boring exercise in the gym, and Blue, who trains six days a week, lasted nine seconds before his hands opened. But the dead hang does three jobs most workouts never touch: your shoulders, your spine and your grip.

Your shoulders: everything we train is in front of us, and our arms almost never go all the way overhead holding our weight. For years, a common fix for shoulder pain was surgery that shaves bone off the top of the shoulder. Then doctors in Britain tested it against fake surgery, and after six months it did no better. In Finland, ten years later, still no difference. In an MRI, pulling a raised arm down against resistance made the gap above the tendon wider than pushing it up, in some positions more than double. The active hang trains a very similar pull-down.

Your spine: when you hang, your legs stop pressing down on your spine and start pulling on it. Twenty minutes of traction made people a few millimeters taller, but it was gone about half an hour after they stood back up. So a hang is a break between hours in a chair, not a back rebuild. The real refill happens at night, when your discs soak water back up.

Your grip: in a study of almost 140,000 adults in 17 countries, every 11 lb (5 kg) weaker grip went with a 16% higher risk of dying over four years, and grip predicted it better than blood pressure. A weak grip doesn't kill you. It's the warning light, not the engine.

The 3 levels:

• Level 1 — Passive hang: thumbs wrapped around the bar, hands a little wider than your shoulders, arms straight, body long and still, and breathe. No kicking or swinging. When you can hold it for 60 seconds, move up
• Level 2 — Active hang: from the passive hang, pull your shoulders down, away from your ears, without bending your elbows. Your body rises about an inch. It's not a pull-up, only the very first part of one
• Level 3 — L-sit hang: from the active hang, lift both legs straight out until they're level with your hips. If straight legs are too hard, tuck your knees first

How long is good? In one study, physically active young men hung for about 73 seconds, and motocross riders, who hold on to handlebars every ride, lasted about 113. Just hanging longer isn't enough, though: in climbers, only the group that added a little weight every week got a stronger grip.

Your plan: 3 days a week, at the start of your workout. 3 hangs at your level, as long as you can with clean form, with 1 minute of rest between them. Can't hang for 10 seconds yet? Keep your toes on a box under the bar and push through your feet a little less every week. And never just let go: put your feet down first. Passive until 60 seconds, then active, then the L-sit, and when the L-sit gets easy, hold a light dumbbell between your feet. Blue started at 9 seconds. Five weeks later, he hung for 52.

Under your biceps sits a flat muscle called the brachialis. In MRI scans it's about as big as the biceps itself, and because it sits underneath, a bigger brachialis makes your whole arm thicker. The triceps, on the back of your arm, was about two and a half times bigger than the biceps in those same scans, so that's where most of the size is. Only its long head crosses the shoulder, so it gets the deepest stretch with your arm over your head. In one study, the triceps in the arm trained overhead grew about 40% more after 12 weeks, even with lighter weights. And curls done only in the stretched bottom part grew the biceps more than twice as much as curls done only at the top.

Here's how:

• Width — The hammer curl: palms facing each other the whole time, elbows pinned at your sides. Curl up, squeeze and lower slowly. 3 sets of 10–12
• Height — The dumbbell curl, done properly: start with your arms fully straight, turn your palms up and out as you curl, then lower all the way down until your arm is straight again. Skip the half reps at the top. 3 sets of 8–12
• Depth — The overhead triceps extension: one dumbbell in both hands above your head, elbows close to your ears, lower it behind your head until you feel a deep stretch, then press it back up. 3 sets of 10–12
• No dumbbells? A loaded backpack works for all three moves

The 3 rules that make it work: go close to failure (stop when you've only got one or two clean reps left), beat last week by one more rep or a slightly heavier weight, and train your arms twice a week, not once. That last rep is the easiest one to skip on your own, so find a friend who's starting from zero and make it a race.

Hammer curls for width, dumbbell curls for height, overhead extensions for depth. Give it a few months and your sleeves will start to feel tight. Which part of your arm is the weakest: width, height or depth?

• Let the bar roll down to your fingertips, then curl it back slow
• 5 sets of 8 at 70–80% of your max, 3 days a week, for 6 weeks
• 8 smooth reps? Add weight
• Tape the forearm, never the wrist
